name: For Parents: Thinking For or Helping to Think
title: For Parents: Thinking For or Helping to Think
answer: This idea gives parents a plain way to tell whether AI at school is doing their child's thinking or helping the child think. The ten patterns show that most uses of AI sit with adults doing their own jobs better, and only a few put AI directly in front of students. Those few are the ones to watch, and the signs usually show up at home.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: Parents often ask one simple question about AI in school, whether it is doing their child's thinking or helping the child think. The ten patterns make that question easier to answer because they sort the uses of AI by who is actually working with it. Most patterns, including drafting, logistics, language access and early warning, are about adults using AI to do their own jobs better. Only a few patterns place AI directly in front of students, and those are the ones that deserve attention. The problem this solves is that parents otherwise have no clear way to judge what they see at home.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The signs show up at home rather than in a policy document. A child who can explain the homework in their own words, who revises after feedback, and who can do similar problems without a device is being helped to think. A child who hands in polished work but cannot explain it, or who panics when the tool is unavailable, may be leaning on AI to do the thinking. The book sets these signs side by side in Figure 2.8 so a parent can compare them. The text does not give separate guidance by grade band.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, no measurement and no evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. The only reference it gives is Figure 2.8, which lists the signs of being helped to think and the signs of leaning on AI side by side. That figure is a comparison for parents to use, not a research finding. Readers should treat the guidance here as practical advice rather than as a tested result.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text is clear that the point is not to keep AI away from children, but to make sure it leaves the learning with them. If the signs worry a parent, the first step is the teacher and not the principal. Parents should ask which tools the class uses, how they are set up, and whether there are regular checks without the tool. Most teachers welcome the question because they are watching for the same thing. The judgement about a particular child stays with the people who know that child, the parent and the teacher.
